To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Basal forebrain cholinergic grafts in the hippocampus and frontal neocortex can restore lesion‐induced cholinergic deficits and that graft‐derived acetylcholine release is regulated by behavior and drugs.

(i) the graft‐derived acetylcholine release was increased up to 2.5 times the normal level, and that (ii) graft‐derived ACH release could be regulated by sensory stimulation, immobilisation, motor activity and monoaminergic drugs.
Basal forebrain cholinergic grafts in the hippocampus and neocortex are capable of regulating acetylcholine release in a manner comparable to normal cholinergic projection systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of cell transplantation as a treatment for brain disorders.
the development and functional integration of cholinergic grafts implanted into the hippocampus and neocortex of adult rats.
the functional integration of cholinergic grafts in the adult rat hippocampus or frontal neocortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the basal forebrain neurons transplanted into the hippocampus and neocortex are able to integrate in the host brain and regulate the release of ACh in a manner similar to that of the normal basal cholinergic neurons.

the basal forebrain grafts, when placed in the hippocampus or cortex, are able to release acetylcholine, and this release is regulated by the same mechanisms that regulate acetylcholine release from normal cholinergic neurons.
grafts of fetal basal forebrain tissue to the hippocampus and frontal neocortex are able to release ACh in a regulated manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the graft‐derived cholinergic innervation of the hippocampus and frontal neocortex is functionally integrated with the host brain, and that the graft‐induced ACh release is regulated by behavioral and pharmacological manipulations that are normally effective on the basal forebrain cholinergic projection systems.

the grafts are capable of restoring the cholinergic innervation of the hippocampus and frontal neocortex to levels that allow for a normal or above normal release of transmitter, and that the graft‐derived transmitter release can be regulated in a fashion similar to that of the normal basal cholinergic systems.
the cholinergic neurons of the basal forebrain can be grafted into the hippocampus or the neocortex and that they can be integrated in the host brain to functionally regulate ACh release.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the graft‐derived acetylcholine release is regulated by a number of different factors.
the grafts are functional in the sense that they respond to various behavioral manipulations in a similar fashion as normal cholinergic projection systems.
the grafts can be functionally integrated in the host brain, and that they can restore normal cholinergic activity in a brain area that is severely affected in AD.
